Mitigating Over-squashing without Rewiring:
A Sheaf Effective Resistance Perspective

André Ribeiro    Getulio Vargas Foundation    andre.guimaraes@fgv.br    Germano Barcelos Affiliation: Federal University of Viçosa Email: gegenbarcelos@gmail.com    Amauri H. Souza    Federal Institute of Ceará    2δ\delta AI    amauriholanda@ifce.edu.br    Diego Mesquita    Getulio Vargas Foundation    2δ\delta AI    diego.mesquita@fgv.br    Ana Luiza Tenório    Getulio Vargas Foundation    UFRRJ    anatenorio@ufrrj.br
Abstract

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) often struggle to capture long-range dependencies due to over-squashing — a phenomenon in which the repeated compression of node embeddings into finite-size messages causes representations to collapse. Over-squashing is most often diagnosed as a property of the graph topology, with effective resistance serving as a principled measure of the bottleneck. We provide a complementary view on the matter: building on cellular sheaves, we introduce sheaf effective resistance, a generalization of effective resistance that depends on the sheaf attached to the graph, and we prove that for flat vector bundles, the over-squashing sensitivity in the Jacobian sense is upper bounded by a quantity related to the sheaf effective resistance between the nodes. The bottleneck thus need not lie in the graph itself: it can be relocated, and reduced, by adjusting the sheaf. We instantiate this idea in FlatNSD, a simple message-passing variant of Neural Sheaf Diffusion, and show that it implicitly learns to modulate total sheaf effective resistance, performing well on benchmarks designed to stress over-squashing without altering the original graph topology.

1 Introduction

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have become the dominant approach for learning on relational data, with applications ranging from molecular chemistry (Duvenaud et al., 2015; Gilmer et al., 2017) to recommendation (Ying et al., 2018) and physical simulation (Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020). Their performance, however, is constrained by two well-documented pathologies: over-smoothing, where iterated message passing makes node embeddings nearly indistinguishable, and over-squashing, where information from exponentially many nodes is compressed into fixed-size vectors, hindering long-range dependencies. Recent work by Bodnar et al. (2022) introduced Neural Sheaf Diffusion (NSD), a generalization of Graph Convolutional Networks (Kipf and Welling, 2017) that uses cellular sheaves to mitigate over-smoothing while accommodating heterophilic graphs.

This raises a natural question: can sheaf-based models also mitigate over-squashing? The role of sheaves in this setting has been explored by Bamberger et al. (2025), who introduced flat vector bundles as a scalable parameterization of sheaves and proposed BuNN, a sheaf-inspired architecture that steps outside the message-passing paradigm to address over-squashing. Building on their flat-bundle formulation, we show that the message-passing paradigm itself is sufficient to alleviate over-squashing, and we introduce FlatNSD as a simple NSD variant to support this claim.

Our analysis builds on a tool from the rewiring literature: effective resistance. The prevailing view treats over-squashing as a topological bottleneck. Through a Jacobian sensitivity analysis, Topping et al. (2022) linked the issue to edges of high negative curvature; Black et al. (2023) introduced effective resistance as a metric for over-squashing and proposed adding edges to reduce it; and Di Giovanni et al. (2023) further showed that over-squashing primarily affects distant nodes. Together, these works established graph topology as the main driver of over-squashing.

On the other hand, we have sheaves: a cellular sheaf ℱ{\mathcal{F}} on a fixed graph is mathematical structure that assigns a vector space, the stalk, to each vertex and edge, together with linear restriction maps for each incident vertex–edge pair. Whereas Hansen and Gebhart (2020) considered fixed restriction maps, Bodnar et al. (2022) proposed learning them end-to-end, yielding a flexible model that adapts to the task. Information propagation in NSD is governed by the sheaf Laplacian, which generalizes the graph Laplacian and is determined by the restriction maps. This suggests a different perspective on over-squashing: the graph itself need not be modified; one can instead adjust the sheaf ℱ{\mathcal{F}} assigned to it. Intuitively, restriction maps modulate the communication channels between nodes, so an appropriate choice of ℱ{\mathcal{F}} can play the role traditionally assigned to edge rewiring. This marks a shift in perspective: the bottleneck responsible for over-squashing need not lie in the graph, but in the sheaf attached to it. Rather than asking which edges to add/remove, we ask which restriction maps to learn.

To make this precise, we generalize the classical effective resistance and introduce sheaf effective resistance Rℱ⁡(u,v)\operatorname{R}_{{\mathcal{F}}}(u,v), which quantifies the ease of transferring information between nodes uu and vv on a fixed graph. Our results show that lower Rℱ⁡(u,v)\operatorname{R}_{{\mathcal{F}}}(u,v) corresponds to less compression of messages (Theorem 4.1). Empirically, evaluations on synthetic data reveal a strong inverse relationship between total sheaf effective resistance and predictive accuracy (Figure 2). When using SAGE to learn the restriction maps, FlatNSD produces Laplacians with low sheaf effective resistance and correspondingly higher accuracy (Figure 1). Importantly, as we analyze in Section B.2, our modifications mitigate over-squashing without inducing over-smoothing — addressing a natural concern given the well-known tension between the two phenomena. Our theoretical results extend beyond FlatNSD to a broader class of MPNNs that we refer to as SNNs (see Equation 2).

In summary, our main contributions are the following:

  1. 1.

    We derive closed-form equations for the sheaf effective resistance (Section 4) and prove that the sheaf effective resistance for flat vector bundles upper bounds the over-squashing sensitivity (Theorem 4.1).

  2. 2.

    Through synthetic experiments that control over-squashing, we support the theory observing that accuracy increases while sheaf effective resistance decreases (Figure 1 and Figure 2).

  3. 3.

    Empirical evaluations on real-world tasks show that FlatNSD offers a robust alternative, performing competitively alongside established rewiring and graph transformer baselines.

  4. 4.

    We identify key architectural choices driving SNN performance (i.e., the role of restriction-map parameterization and stalk dimension) providing guidance for future sheaf-based models.

2 Background

In this section, we briefly review cellular sheaves and their use in GNNs. Moreover, we overview how effective resistance was previously studied to avoid over-squashing.

Notation. Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a connected, undirected, unweighted graph with nn vertices and mm edges. Let AA be the adjacency matrix of GG and DD its degree matrix. The graph Laplacian of GG is LG=D−AL_{G}=D-A and its normalized version by ΔG=I−A^=D−1/2LGD−1/2\Delta_{G}=I-\hat{A}=D^{-1/2}L_{G}D^{-1/2}, with A^=D−1/2AD−1/2\hat{A}=D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}.

Cellular Sheaves. A cellular sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F} over a graph GG associates (i) vector spaces ℱ⁡(v)\mathcal{F}(v) and ℱ⁡(e)\mathcal{F}(e) to each vertex v∈Vv\in V and each edge e∈Ee\in E, respectively; (ii) linear maps ℱv⊴e:ℱ⁡(v)→ℱ⁡(e)\mathcal{F}_{v\unlhd e}:\mathcal{F}(v)\to\mathcal{F}(e) to each incident vertex-edge pair v⊴ev\unlhd e. The vector spaces are called stalks, and the linear maps are called restriction maps. For simplicity, it is standard to assume that all stalks are isomorphic to ℝd{\mathbb{R}}^{d}. If d=1d=1 and all restriction maps are the identity map, we have the so called trivial sheaf.

In GNNs, diffusion is often governed by the graph Laplacian. In SNNs, the sheaf Laplacian plays an analogous role, but its definition involves several intermediate steps.

When the sheaf is trivial, this operator coincides with B⊤B^{\top}, where BB is the incidence matrix of GG. Then, the sheaf Laplacian is defined by δ⊤​δ\delta^{\top}\delta, generalizing the Laplacian description as B​B⊤BB^{\top}. Equivalently, we also have that the sheaf Laplacian of ℱ\mathcal{F} is the linear operator Lℱ:C0​(G,ℱ)→C0​(G,ℱ)L_{\mathcal{F}}:C^{0}(G,\mathcal{F})\to C^{0}(G,\mathcal{F}) given by Lℱ​(𝐗)v:=∑v,u⊴eℱv⊴e⊤​(ℱv⊴e​𝐱v−ℱu⊴e​𝐱u),∀v∈V.L_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathbf{X})_{v}:=\sum_{v,u\unlhd e}\mathcal{F}_{v\unlhd e}^{\top}\left(\mathcal{F}_{v\unlhd e}\mathbf{x}_{v}-\mathcal{F}_{u\unlhd e}\mathbf{x}_{u}\right),\forall v\in V.

It can also be written as Lℱ=Dℱ−AℱL_{{\mathcal{F}}}=D_{{\mathcal{F}}}-A_{{\mathcal{F}}}, where DℱD_{{\mathcal{F}}} is the block-diagonal sheaf-degree matrix, and AℱA_{{\mathcal{F}}} the sheaf-adjacency matrix. Its normalized version is Δℱ=Dℱ−12​Lℱ​Dℱ−12\Delta_{{\mathcal{F}}}=D_{{\mathcal{F}}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}L_{{\mathcal{F}}}D_{{\mathcal{F}}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}.

Neural Sheaf Diffusion (NSD). One of the first, and currently the most popular SNN model was introduced in Bodnar et al. (2022) as follows:

𝐇t+1=𝐇t−σ⁡(Δℱ⁡(t)​(𝐈⊗𝐖1,t)​𝐇t​𝐖2,t),\mathbf{H}_{t+1}=\mathbf{H}_{t}-\sigma(\Delta_{{\mathcal{F}}(t)}(\mathbf{I}\otimes\mathbf{W}_{1,t})\mathbf{H}_{t}\mathbf{W}_{2,t}), (1)

where 𝐇0∈ℝn​d×h\mathbf{H}_{0}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{nd\times h} is the matrix of initial node features projected into hh channels, 𝐖1,t\mathbf{W}_{1,t} and 𝐖2,t\mathbf{W}_{2,t} are weight square matrices of dimensions dd and hh, respectively, ⊗\otimes is the Kronecker product, and σ\sigma is an activation. Furthermore, the Laplacian is learned locally through the graph features: each restriction map Fv⊴eF_{v\unlhd e} is learned using a function Φ:ℝ2​d→ℝd×d\Phi:\mathbb{R}^{2d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, with ℱv⊴e≔(v,u)=Φ⁡(𝐱v,𝐱u){\mathcal{F}}_{v\unlhd e\coloneqq(v,u)}=\Phi(\mathbf{x}_{v},\mathbf{x}_{u}).

Classes of sheaves. Bodnar et al. (2022) studied three classes of sheaves based on the properties of their restriction maps: diagonal, orthogonal, and general (i.e, any invertible linear map). The best balance between scalability and empirical performance was achieved by orthogonal restriction maps. We call this class of sheaves vector bundles. More recently, further improving the computational complexity of SNNs, Bamberger et al. (2025) presented flat vector bundles as part of their Bundle Neural Networks (BuNNs) model. They consider the special case of flat vector bundles in which to every node vv is assigned an orthogonal map ℱv{\mathcal{F}}_{v}, which replaces ℱv⊴e\mathcal{F}_{v\unlhd e} for any adjacent edge ee. Instead of building the model directly over the sheaf Laplacian, BuNN uses the bundle heat kernel.

Effective Resistance. Originally defined by Kirchhoff (1847), effective resistance is the voltage difference between two points in an electrical network when a unit current is applied. In the realm of GNNs, it serves as a measure of proximity and connectivity within a graph, and it was recently incorporated to mitigate over-squashing (Black et al., 2023). Formally, the effective resistance between nodes uu and vv is defined by R⁡(u,v)=(1u−1v)⊤​LG+​(1u−1v),\operatorname{R}(u,v)=(1_{u}-1_{v})^{\top}L^{+}_{G}(1_{u}-1_{v}), where 1v1_{v} is an indicator vector, i.e., a binary vector of length nn and in this vector, only the entry corresponding to node vv is 11, and L+L^{+} is the pseudo-inverse of the graph Laplacian.

Over-squashing. The connection between over-squashing and effective resistance passes through the work from Topping et al. (2022), which proposed an upper bound on the 22-norm of the Jacobian between node features, ‖∂hu(r)/∂xv‖\|\partial h^{(r)}_{u}/\partial x_{v}\|, with hu(r)h^{(r)}_{u} and xvx_{v} both being vectors. This Jacobian quantifies how the initial feature xvx_{v} at node vv affects hu(r)h^{(r)}_{u} at node uu in the rr-th GNN layer. Then, Black et al. (2023) proved that if R⁡(u,v)\operatorname{R}(u,v) decreases, then the upper bound increases, allowing for an improved information flow between uu and vv. More precisely, using ϕt\phi_{t} and ψt\psi_{t} to denote, respectively, learnable update and message functions at layer tt, they obtained:

Theorem 2.1 (Theorem 3.3 Black et al. (2023)).

Let GG be a non-bipartite graph, and let u,v∈Vu,v\in V. Suppose ‖∇ϕl‖≤α\|\nabla\phi_{l}\|\leq\alpha and max⁡{‖∇ψl‖,1}≤β\max\{\|\nabla\psi_{l}\|,1\}\leq\beta. Define dmin=min⁡{du,dv}d_{\min}=\min\{d_{u},d_{v}\} and dmax=max⁡{du,dv}d_{\max}=\max\{d_{u},d_{v}\}. Let max⁡{|μ2|,…,|μn|}≤μ\max\{|\mu_{2}|,...,|\mu_{n}|\}\leq\mu. Then

‖∂hu(r)∂xv‖≤(2​α​β)r​dm​a​x2​(2dm​i​n​(r+1+μr+11−μ)−R⁡(u,v)).\left\|\frac{\partial h_{u}^{(r)}}{\partial x_{v}}\right\|\leq(2\alpha\beta)^{r}\frac{d_{max}}{2}\left(\dfrac{2}{d_{min}}\left(r+1+\frac{\mu^{r+1}}{1-\mu}\right)-\operatorname{R}(u,v)\right).

Black et al. (2023) rewiring technique adds new edges between certain nodes, aiming to decrease the total effective resistance — the sum of the effective resistances between all pairs of nodes. This brings significant improvements in empirical results when compared with GNNs with no rewiring.

Rewiring is a standard method to address over-squashing by improving the connectivity of a graph and potentially easing structural bottlenecks. Its general goal is to create new connections that enable a more efficient and balanced flow of information within the network. We focus on the comparison with Black et al. (2023) because they also work with effective resistance but other strategies can be applied: for instance, spectral gap (Karhadkar et al., 2023; Banerjee et al., 2022), or different notions of curvature (Fesser and Weber, 2024; Giraldo et al., 2023).

3 Sheaf Neural Networks via Message Passing

We analyze over-squashing through the lens of the Jacobian, in the same fashion as Theorem 2.1. Therefore, we need to describe the NSD model in the message passing framework.

Recall that for a graph whose nodes uu have neighborhoods Nu={v∈V|(v,u)∈E}N_{u}\!=\!\{v\!\in\!V\,|\,(v,u)\!\in\!E\} and features hu(0)=xu\textbf{h}_{u}^{(0)}\!\!=\!\textbf{x}_{u}, a message passing layer is defined as hv(t+1)=ϕt​(hv(t),⨁u∈Nvψt​(hu(t),hv(t)))\textbf{h}^{(t+1)}_{v}\!=\!\phi_{t}\!\!\left(\textbf{h}^{(t)}_{v}\!\!,\bigoplus_{u\in N_{v}}\!\!\psi_{t}\!\left(\!\textbf{h}^{(t)}_{u},\textbf{h}^{(t)}_{v}\!\right)\!\!\right), where ψt\psi_{t} is the message function, ϕt\phi_{t} is the update function, and ⊕\oplus is a permutation-invariant aggregation function.

The NSD model described in Equation 1 is a message-passing GNN where the message function is updated for each layer since it is given by ψt​(hu,hv)=Dv−12​ℱv⊴e⊤​(ℱv⊴e​Dv−12​𝐡v−ℱu⊴e​Du−12​𝐡u)\psi_{t}(\textbf{h}_{u},\textbf{h}_{v})=D_{v}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathcal{F}_{v\unlhd e}^{\top}\left(\mathcal{F}_{v\unlhd e}D_{v}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{h}_{v}-\mathcal{F}_{u\unlhd e}D_{u}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{h}_{u}\right), if we ignore the weights, and the aggregation is the sum. This simple observation provides significantly more efficient implementation and accommodates directed graph inputs, which the original code from Bodnar et al. (2022) does not. Moreover, if ℱ{\mathcal{F}} is a flat vector bundle, then

Dv−12​ℱv⊤​ℱu​Du−12=1du​dv​ℱv⊤​ℱu=A^u​v​ℱv⊤​ℱu.D_{v}^{-\frac{1}{2}}{\mathcal{F}}_{v}^{\top}{\mathcal{F}}_{u}D_{u}^{-\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{u}d_{v}}}{\mathcal{F}}_{v}^{\top}{\mathcal{F}}_{u}=\hat{A}_{uv}{\mathcal{F}}_{v}^{\top}{\mathcal{F}}_{u}.

Thus, we can write the FlatNSD model, which is NSD restricted to flat vector bundles, as

hv(t+1)=ϕt​(hv(t),∑u∈NvA^u​v​ψt​(hu(t))),\textbf{h}^{(t+1)}_{v}=\phi_{t}\left(\textbf{h}^{(t)}_{v},\sum\limits_{u\in N_{v}}\hat{A}_{uv}\psi_{t}\left(\textbf{h}^{(t)}_{u}\right)\right), (2)

where ψt​(hu)=−ℱu​hu\psi_{t}(\textbf{h}_{u})=-{\mathcal{F}}_{u}\textbf{h}_{u}, up to weight matrices, A^u​v\hat{A}_{uv} is the normalized adjacency matrix of the graph, and ℱv⊤{\mathcal{F}}_{v}^{\top} is applied by ϕt\phi_{t}, since ℱv{\mathcal{F}}_{v} is linear. Therefore, the FlatNSD model is a Message Passing Neural Network (MPNN) that fits in the framework explored by Black et al. (2023), allowing us to apply some of their results. In the following sections, we show that restricting attention to flat vector bundles yields additional computational and theoretical benefits. In Appendix C, we provide a summary with our main contributions, distinguishing what is novel from prior work. We also provide a comparison of FlatNSD with existing sheaf architectures to better highlight its role as a tool to empirically verify our theoretical claims rather than a novel model.

4 Sheaf effective resistance

We introduce sheaf effective resistance (sheaf ER) and theoretically connect it with over-squashing.

Definition 4.1.

The sheaf effective resistance between nodes uu and vv is defined by

Rℱ⁡(u,v)=(𝟙u−𝟙v)⊤​Lℱ+​(𝟙u−𝟙v),\operatorname{R}_{\mathcal{F}}(u,v)=(\mathbbm{1}_{u}-\mathbbm{1}_{v})^{\top}L_{\mathcal{F}}^{+}(\mathbbm{1}_{u}-\mathbbm{1}_{v}),

where 𝟙v\mathbbm{1}_{v} is a vector of dimension n​dnd where the dd entries corresponding to node vv is 11. Lℱ+L_{\mathcal{F}}^{+} is the pseudo-inverse of the sheaf Laplacian.

If ℱ\mathcal{F} is the trivial sheaf, then d=1d=1 and sheaf effective resistance coincides with effective resistance.

Example 4.1.

Consider the graph with only two vertices uu and vv, and an edge ee between them.

  1. 1.

    If ℱ\mathcal{F} is the trivial sheaf, then Rℱ​(u,v)=R⁡(u,v)=1.R_{\mathcal{F}}(u,v)=R(u,v)=1.

  2. 2.

    If ℱ{\mathcal{F}} is a sheaf such that all stalks are isomorphic to ℝ2{\mathbb{R}}^{2}, ℱu⊴e=(cos⁡(x)−sin⁡(x)sin⁡(x)cos⁡(x))\mathcal{F}_{u\unlhd e}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos(x)&-\sin(x)\\ \sin(x)&\cos(x)\end{pmatrix}, and ℱv⊴e=(cos⁡(y)−sin⁡(y)sin⁡(y)cos⁡(y))\mathcal{F}_{v\unlhd e}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos(y)&-\sin(y)\\ \sin(y)&\cos(y)\end{pmatrix}, then Rℱ​(u,v)=cos⁡(x−y)+1R_{{\mathcal{F}}}(u,v)=\cos(x-y)+1.

In Appendix E, we provide more details to perform the calculations above. Observe that by simply changing the sheaf, without changing the graph, we can reduce or increase the effective resistance depending only on the restriction maps. Larger worked examples can be found in Appendix A

From now on, we focus on flat vector bundles, deriving formulas for their effective resistance and proving the relationship with over-squashing sensitivity. Importantly, this restriction is highly practical: prior work shows vector bundles optimally balance scalability and performance (Bodnar et al., 2022), with the flat constraint further enhancing efficiency (Bamberger et al., 2025). Additionally, our preliminary experiments with general sheaves revealed significant numerical instability. Thus, flat vector bundles emerge as the most robust and practical choice for sheaf-based networks.

First, observe that for flat vector bundles, the sheaf Laplacian can be written as Lℱ=𝐎⊤​(LG⊗Id)​𝐎L_{{\mathcal{F}}}={\mathbf{O}}^{\top}(L_{G}\otimes I_{d}){\mathbf{O}}, where 𝐎=blockdiag⁡(ℱ1,ℱ2,…,ℱn)∈ℝn​d×n​d{\mathbf{O}}=\operatorname{blockdiag}({\mathcal{F}}_{1},{\mathcal{F}}_{2},\dots,{\mathcal{F}}_{n})\in{\mathbb{R}}^{nd\times nd} (Bamberger et al., 2025). In the following, we consider a flat vector bundle ℱ{\mathcal{F}} over GG and LGL_{G} the graph Laplacian.

Proposition 4.1.

The pseudo-inverse of LℱL_{{\mathcal{F}}} is Lℱ+=𝐎⊤​(LG+⊗Id)​𝐎L_{{\mathcal{F}}}^{+}={\mathbf{O}}^{\top}(L_{G}^{+}\otimes I_{d}){\mathbf{O}}.

Crucially, this provides the following formula to compute Rℱ​(u,v)R_{{\mathcal{F}}}(u,v).

Proposition 4.2.

Let 𝟏d∈ℝd\mathbf{1}_{d}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} be a vector of ones, and Mu​v=𝟏d⊤​ℱu⊤​ℱv​𝟏dM_{uv}=\mathbf{1}_{d}^{\top}{\mathcal{F}}_{u}^{\top}{\mathcal{F}}_{v}\mathbf{1}_{d}. Then

Rℱ⁡(u,v)=d⁡((LG+)u​u+(LG+)v​v)−2​Mu​v​(LG+)u​v.\operatorname{R}_{\mathcal{F}}(u,v)=d((L_{G}^{+})_{uu}+(L_{G}^{+})_{vv})-2M_{uv}(L_{G}^{+})_{uv}.

If ℱ{\mathcal{F}} is the trivial sheaf, we obtain R⁡(u,v)=(LG+)u​u+(LG+)v​v−2​(LG+)u​v\operatorname{R}(u,v)=(L_{G}^{+})_{uu}+(L_{G}^{+})_{vv}-2(L_{G}^{+})_{uv}. So we have generalized a classical result. Importantly, this also allows us to write Rℱ⁡(u,v)\operatorname{R}_{\mathcal{F}}(u,v) in terms of R⁡(u,v)\operatorname{R}(u,v):

Rℱ⁡(u,v)=d​R⁡(u,v)+2​(d−Mu​v)​(LG+)u​v.\operatorname{R}_{\mathcal{F}}(u,v)=d\operatorname{R}(u,v)+2(d-M_{uv})(L_{G}^{+})_{uv}. (3)

Note that computing RℱR_{{\mathcal{F}}} requires only a single pseudo-inverse calculation, as the sheaf effective resistance for any flat vector bundle ℱ{\mathcal{F}} depends on the pseudo-inverse of the graph Laplacian, which remains unchanged since we do not rewire the graph.

Theorem 4.1 below formalizes the relationship between sheaf effective resistance and over-squashing.

Theorem 4.1.

Let GG be a non-bipartite graph, and let u,v∈Vu,v\in V. Suppose ‖∇ϕl‖≤α\|\nabla\phi_{l}\|\leq\alpha and max⁡{‖∇ψt‖,1}|≤β\max\{\|\nabla\psi_{t}\|,1\}|\leq\beta. Define dmin=min⁡{du,dv}d_{\min}=\min\{d_{u},d_{v}\}, dmax=max⁡{du,dv}d_{\max}=\max\{d_{u},d_{v}\}, and fix dd the dimension of the stalks. Let max⁡{|μ2|,…,|μn|}≤μ\max\{|\mu_{2}|,...,|\mu_{n}|\}\leq\mu. If (LG+)u​v≥0(L_{G}^{+})_{uv}\geq 0, then

‖∂hu(r)∂xv‖≤(2αβ)rdm​a​x2(2dm​i​n(r+1+μr+11−μ)+4(LG+)u​v−Rℱ⁡(u,v)d).\left\|\frac{\partial h_{u}^{(r)}}{\partial x_{v}}\right\|\leq(2\alpha\beta)^{r}\frac{d_{max}}{2}\Biggl(\frac{2}{d_{min}}\Biggr(r+1+\frac{\mu^{r+1}}{1-\mu}\Biggr)+4(L_{G}^{+})_{uv}-\frac{\operatorname{R}_{{\mathcal{F}}}(u,v)}{d}\Biggr).

If (LG+)u​v<0(L_{G}^{+})_{uv}<0, then

‖∂hu(r)∂xv‖≤(2αβ)rdm​a​x2(2dm​i​n(r+1+μr+11−μ)−Rℱ⁡(u,v)d).\left\|\frac{\partial h_{u}^{(r)}}{\partial x_{v}}\right\|\leq(2\alpha\beta)^{r}\frac{d_{max}}{2}\Biggl(\frac{2}{d_{min}}\Biggr(r+1+\frac{\mu^{r+1}}{1-\mu}\Biggr)-\frac{\operatorname{R}_{{\mathcal{F}}}(u,v)}{d}\Biggr).

Theorem 4.1 shows that the propagation of messages can be controlled by the sheaf effective resistance. If the sheaf is fixed (the absence of a sheaf is equivalent to fixing the trivial sheaf), we must alter the graph to decrease the effective resistance. However, with varying sheaves, we can keep the original graph and decrease the sheaf effective resistance. Moreover, this provides a perspective change: effective resistance measures communication capacity of the sheaf associated to the graph rather than to the graph itself.

To align theory with experiments, we calculate total sheaf effective resistance Rℱ\operatorname{R}_{{\mathcal{F}}}, i.e., the sum of the sheaf effective resistance Rℱ⁡(u,v)\operatorname{R}_{{\mathcal{F}}}(u,v) for all pairs of nodes. In the following, R\operatorname{R} denotes the total (graph) effective resistance.

Theorem 4.2.

Let ⟨⋅,⋅⟩F\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{F} denote the Frobenius inner product and MM as in Proposition 4.2. Then

Rℱ=d​n​Tr⁡(LG+)−⟨M,LG+⟩F=d​R−⟨M,LG+⟩F.\operatorname{R}_{\mathcal{F}}=dn\operatorname{Tr}(L_{G}^{+})-\langle M,L_{G}^{+}\rangle_{F}=d\operatorname{R}-\langle M,L_{G}^{+}\rangle_{F}.

Importantly, if ℱ{\mathcal{F}} is the trivial sheaf, we obtain R=n​Tr⁡(LG+)\operatorname{R}=n\operatorname{Tr}(L_{G}^{+}). This is another classical result, so our approach is well-founded. We use the above in our implementation to analyze the total sheaf effective resistance in our experiments, using M=S​S⊤M=SS^{\top}, where Su=𝟏d⊤​ℱu⊤S_{u}=\mathbf{1}_{d}^{\top}{\mathcal{F}}_{u}^{\top}. This allows us to calculate the Frobenius inner product using the cyclic property of the trace while avoiding building MM. Furthermore, we characterize when flat bundles strictly decrease sheaf effective resistance.

Proposition 4.3.

Let GG be a connected graph with at least two nodes and ℱ{\mathcal{F}} a flat O⁡(d)O(d)-bundle over GG. Then Rℱd≤R\frac{R_{{\mathcal{F}}}}{d}\leq R, with equality holding if and only if ℱv​𝟏d=c{\mathcal{F}}_{v}\mathbf{1}_{d}=c for some c∈ℝdc\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} and all v∈Vv\in V. In particular, for every d≥1d\geq 1, there exists a flat O⁡(d)O(d)-bundle ℱ{\mathcal{F}} such that Rℱd<R\frac{R_{{\mathcal{F}}}}{d}<R.

We proceed with a corollary of Theorem 4.1 regarding the total sheaf effective resistance.

Corollary 4.1.

Let GG be a non-bipartite graph, and let u,v∈Vu,v\in V. Suppose ‖∇ϕl‖≤α\|\nabla\phi_{l}\|\leq\alpha and max⁡{‖∇ψt‖,1}|≤β\max\{\|\nabla\psi_{t}\|,1\}|\leq\beta. Let dmin=min⁡{du,dv}d_{\min}=\min\{d_{u},d_{v}\}, dmax=max⁡{du,dv}d_{\max}=\max\{d_{u},d_{v}\}, and dd be the minimum stalk dimension. Let max⁡{|μ2|,…,|μn|}≤μ\max\{|\mu_{2}|,...,|\mu_{n}|\}\leq\mu. Then

∑u≠v‖∂hu(r)∂xv‖≤(2αβ)rdm​a​x2(n⁡(n−1)dm​i​n(r+1+μr+11−μ)−Rℱd).\begin{split}{{\sum}}\limits_{u\neq v}\left\|\frac{\partial h_{u}^{(r)}}{\partial x_{v}}\right\|&\leq(2\alpha\beta)^{r}\frac{d_{max}}{2}\Biggl(\dfrac{n(n-1)}{d_{min}}\Biggr(r+1+\frac{\mu^{r+1}}{1-\mu}\Biggr)-\frac{\operatorname{R}_{{\mathcal{F}}}}{d}\Biggr).\end{split}

Importantly, FlatNSD does not require computing the sheaf ER or any pseudo-inverse. Rather, we use the sheaf ER as an analytical tool to understand the performance of our FlatNSD model, since Rℱ⁡(u,v)\operatorname{R}_{{\mathcal{F}}}(u,v) is related to ‖∂hu(r)/∂xv‖\left\|\nicefrac{{\partial h_{u}^{(r)}}}{{\partial x_{v}}}\right\|, which measures sensitivity to over-squashing.

In the previous results, we assumed non-bipartite graphs, similar to Black et al. (2023). We now provide extensions relating graph ER to the Jacobian of MP-based GNNs as in Equation 2 to bipartite graphs, with natural extensions to sheaf ER. We begin by constructing a formula for the Laplacian pseudo-inverse on bipartite graphs.

Lemma 4.1.

Let GG be a connected bipartite graph. Then ΔG+=12​P−+∑k=0∞(A^k−P+−(−1)k​P−)\Delta_{G}^{+}=\frac{1}{2}P_{-}+\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(\hat{A}^{k}-P_{+}-(-1)^{k}P_{-}), where P+P_{+} and P−P_{-} are the outer product of the eigenvectors with eigenvalues 11 and −1-1, respectively.

The next step is to find a formula for the effective resistance of bipartite graphs.

Proposition 4.4.

Let GG be a connected bipartite graph, bu​v=𝟙u−𝟙vb_{uv}=\mathbbm{1}_{u}-\mathbbm{1}_{v}, zu​v=D−1/2bu​vz_{uv}=D^{-1/2}b_{uv}, and γu​v=zu​v⊤​P−​zu​v\gamma_{uv}=z_{uv}^{\top}P_{-}z_{uv}. Then

R⁡(u,v)=γu​v2+∑k=0∞((A^k)u​udu+(A^k)v​vdv−2​(A^k)u​vdu​dv−(−1)k​γu​v)R(u,v)=\frac{\gamma_{uv}}{2}+\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{(\hat{A}^{k})_{uu}}{d_{u}}+\frac{(\hat{A}^{k})_{vv}}{d_{v}}-\frac{2(\hat{A}^{k})_{uv}}{\sqrt{d_{u}d_{v}}}-(-1)^{k}\gamma_{uv}\right)

Now, we proceed to relate the above formula for the effective resistance with the Jacobian bound.

Theorem 4.3.

Let GG be a connected bipartite graph. Let u,v∈V=U⊔Wu,v\!\in\!V=U\!\sqcup\!W, ‖∇ϕl‖≤α\|\nabla\phi_{l}\|\!\leq\!\alpha and max{∥∇ψl∥,1∥≤β\max\{\|\nabla\psi_{l}\|,1\|\leq\beta, dmin=min⁡{du,dv}d_{\min}=\min\{d_{u},d_{v}\}, dmax=max⁡{du,dv}d_{\max}=\max\{d_{u},d_{v}\}, and μ¯=maxi≠1⁡|μi|<1\overline{\mu}=\max_{i\neq 1}|\mu_{i}|<1. Then

‖∂hu(r)∂xv‖≤(2​α​β)r​dmax2​(2dmin​(r+1+μ¯r+11−μ¯)+12​γu​v−R⁡(u,v)).\left\|\frac{\partial h_{u}^{(r)}}{\partial x_{v}}\right\|\leq(2\alpha\beta)^{r}\frac{d_{\max}}{2}\left(\frac{2}{d_{\min}}\left(r+1+\frac{\overline{\mu}^{r+1}}{1-\overline{\mu}}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\gamma_{uv}-R(u,v)\right).

The corollary for the total effective resistance follows from this theorem, where the additional term accounting for bipartiteness becomes 4​|U|​|W|vol⁡(G)\frac{4|U||W|}{\operatorname{vol}(G)} (see Remark E.1).

Remark 4.1 (Geometric interpretation under isospectrality).

A natural question arises from the decomposition Lℱ=𝐎⊤​(LG⊗Id)​𝐎L_{{\mathcal{F}}}={\mathbf{O}}^{\top}(L_{G}\otimes I_{d}){\mathbf{O}}: how can FlatNSD mitigate over-squashing if its diffusion operator has essentially the same spectral properties as the graph Laplacian? The key lies in the rotations performed by the restriction maps. Define ξ=𝟏dd\xi=\frac{\mathbf{1}_{d}}{\sqrt{d}} and gv=ℱv​ξ∈𝕊d−1g_{v}={\mathcal{F}}_{v}\xi\in{\mathbb{S}}^{d-1}. Then

Mu​v=𝟏d⊤ℱu⊤ℱv𝟏d=dξ⊤ℱu⊤ℱvξ=dgu⊤gv=dcosθu​v,M_{uv}=\mathbf{1}_{d}^{\top}{\mathcal{F}}_{u}^{\top}{\mathcal{F}}_{v}\mathbf{1}_{d}=d\xi^{\top}{\mathcal{F}}_{u}^{\top}{\mathcal{F}}_{v}\xi=dg_{u}^{\top}g_{v}=d\cos\theta_{uv},

where θu​v\theta_{uv} is the angle between gug_{u} and gvg_{v}. Thus, Proposition 4.2 can be rewritten as Rℱ⁡(u,v)=d⁡((LG+)u​u+(LG+)v​v−2​cos⁡(θu​v)​(LG+)u​v).\operatorname{R}_{\mathcal{F}}(u,v)=d\big((L_{G}^{+})_{uu}+(L_{G}^{+})_{vv}-2\cos(\theta_{uv})(L_{G}^{+})_{uv}\big). When gu=gvg_{u}=g_{v}, we recover the effective resistance of the trivial dd-dimensional flat bundle. If gu⟂gvg_{u}\perp g_{v}, the cross-term disappears, reducing effective resistance relative to the aligned configuration when (LG+)u​v<0(L_{G}^{+})_{uv}<0. In this case, gu=−gvg_{u}=-g_{v} gives the largest reduction. When (LG+)u​v>0(L_{G}^{+})_{uv}>0, alignment minimizes the effective resistance.

5 Synthetic Experiments

In this section, we test FlatNSD on three different synthetic datasets designed to address over-squashing. Our goal is to endorse that a simple SNN such as FlatNSD can alleviate it. We provide experiments on the short-range over-squashing regime (Mishayev et al., 2025) in Section B.5.

TreeNeighborsMatch. To test FlatNSD ability to deal with over-squashing, we reproduce the TreeNeighborsMatch problem proposed by Alon and Yahav (2021), using the same framework. The TreeNeighborsMatch is a synthetic dataset aimed at evaluating a GNN’s ability to handle over-squashing, assessed through training performance. The underlying graph is a binary tree of depth rr, and the task requires propagating information from the leaves to the root. Both the root and each leaf are attached to a set of blue neighbors. The target label is determined by the unique leaf whose number of blue neighbors matches that of the root. We provide the parameters used for this task in Table 4. In Figure 1, we evaluate FlatNSD under two parameterizations of the restriction maps: an MLP (as in NSD) and SAGE (as in BuNN and CSNN Ribeiro et al. (2026)). FlatNSD-SAGE outperforms all classical baselines (GCN, GIN, GAT, GGNN) as well as BuNN, matching the perfect accuracy of CSNN, a concurrent sheaf-based model. As a point of comparison, NSD with orthogonal maps attains 0.910.91 accuracy at r=3r=3 and 0.050.05 at r=4r=4. To better understand how and why FlatNSD improves performance on this task, we provide an additional experiment with a controlled intervention on this task in Section B.6

Effective Resistance. By Theorem 4.1, lower sheaf ER reduces sensitivity to over-squashing. Consequently, we expect a strong inverse relationship between accuracy and total ER in the TreeNeighborsMatch task, measured via Spearman correlation (Figure 2). For r=8r=8, FlatNSD-SAGE reaches 100% accuracy using both d=2d=2 and d=4d=4. However, d=4d=4 converges much faster (25 steps vs. 143 for d=2d=2) and maintains a strong inverse correlation across all layers. The weaker correlation for d=2d=2 reflects its slower convergence, indicating the model struggles to approximate an optimal sheaf. Full results for all rr are detailed in Section B.4, together with Spearman correlation between Jacobian norm and total sheaf ER.

We further substantiate that FlatNSD mitigates over-squashing by testing its performance on ECHO-Synth (Miglior et al., 2025) and Graph Transfer (Di Giovanni et al., 2023), both capturing long-range interactions.

ECHO-Synth. The ECHO-Synth dataset challenges GNNs with long-range tasks across six topological families (diameters 17–40). Since this setting induces different types of structural compression, it is ideal for evaluating FlatNSD’s capacity to alleviate over-squashing. Following Miglior et al. (2025), we benchmark FlatNSD against their original models, with the addition of CSNN (Ribeiro et al., 2026) to assess the capacity of a recent, more engineered sheaf model. We use the same experimental setup and hyperparameter selection routine (details in Appendix F).

Results. Table 1 reports MAE across the three property prediction tasks. FlatNSDSAGE{}_{\text{SAGE}} demonstrates reliable effectiveness in handling long-range dependencies, establishing an impressive performance on the ecc task, outperforming the next best baseline (CSNN) by over 30%. Furthermore, it consistently ranks among the top performers on the remaining tasks, securing the third-best result on sssp and remaining highly competitive on diam. These results confirm FlatNSD’s capacity to effectively alleviate over-squashing across diverse structural bottlenecks. Furthermore, CSNN is also effective in these tasks, achieving the lowest MAE on diam and sssp, highlighting the effectiveness of a more intricate sheaf-based model regarding over-squashing mitigation.

Graph Transfer. We consider three graph topologies (CrossedRing, Ring, and CliquePath), each parameterized by the shortest-path distance rr between a designated source–target pair. The target node is assigned a one-hot label, and every other node receives a constant unitary feature. The model is trained to reproduce the target’s label at the source. Since information must travel a distance rr through the graph, this task isolates over-squashing as the dominant failure mode, with accuracy expected to decrease as rr grows.

Results. Figure 3 shows that with FlatNSD accuracy decreases after longer distances from source to target, in comparison with GCN and SAGE, for all three topologies. In Section B.3, we show that FlatNSD also outperforms GIN and GAT, and discuss that for d=4d=4 the performance is better than for d=2d=2, suggesting the importance of stalk dimension on tasks sensitive to over-squashing, in alignment with our results for the TreeNeighborsMatch (Figure 1).

6 Real-world experiments

Node Classification. To further show that sheaf models are a robust alternative, we also evaluate FlatNSD on the five heterophilic graphs proposed by Platonov et al. (2023). For binary classification datasets, we report AUROC, while for multiclass datasets we report accuracy.

Following Platonov et al. (2023), who showed that classical GNNs often match or outperform architectures specifically designed for heterophilic graphs, we adopt their reference baselines: GCN (Kipf and Welling, 2017), GraphSAGE (Hamilton et al., 2017), GAT (Veličković et al., 2017), and GT (Shi et al., 2020), together with the GAT-sep and GT-sep variants, which concatenate a node’s representation with the mean of its neighbors rather than summing them (Zhu et al., 2020). We also compare FlatNSD against the recently proposed sheaf models BuNN (Bamberger et al., 2025), and CSNN (Ribeiro et al., 2026). All three sheaf models considered use SAGE to learn the restriction maps.

Result. As shown in Table 2, sheaf-based models are uniformly robust on heterophilic datasets. While more sophisticated variants surpass FlatNSD — BuNN by departing from the message-passing paradigm, and CSNN by coupling two cooperative sheaves to refine node communication within message passing — FlatNSD remains within close range of both. This supports our broader claim: the message-passing paradigm itself, when equipped with appropriate restriction maps, is already sufficient to alleviate over-squashing.

Graph classification. We validate our theoretical claims through the Spearman correlation of sheaf effective resistance and accuracy on graph classification graphs Enzymes, IMDB, Mutag, and Proteins from the TUDatasets Morris et al. (2020). Our objective is to elucidate how cellular sheaves can alleviate over-squashing without changing the topology of the graph, but rather the structure of its underlying sheaf. In Table 3 we conduct the same analysis for small graphs with a node classification task for Cora, Citeseer Yang et al. (2016), Texas, Cornell, Wisconsin Pei et al. (2020), and Chameleon Rozemberczki et al. (2021).

Experimental setup. Aiming to prioritize fairness and understandability instead of obtaining the highest accuracy, we follow Nguyen et al. (2023); Liang et al. (2025), that tune only rewiring-related hyperparameters, and freeze GNN-specific parameters and tune only the sheaf-related ones. We compare FlatNSD against GCN, GIN, SAGE, and seven rewiring methods using these three GNNs as backbone models: SDRF Topping et al. (2022), FOSR Karhadkar et al. (2023), BORF Nguyen et al. (2023), DR Attali et al. (2024), GTR Black et al. (2023), LASER Barbero et al. (2024), and GOKU Liang et al. (2025). Appendix F provides details on our experimental setup.

Effective Resistance. We use Spearman rank correlation coefficient to measure the correlation between accuracy and effective resistance. Since real-world data faces multiple challenges beyond requiring over-squashing mitigation, we do not expect the inverse relation to be as strong as in the controlled synthetic experiment reported in Figure 2. Nevertheless, the effective resistance is considerably correlated with training accuracy in these datasets, in alignment with the theory we developed.

Results. Figure 5 demonstrates that FlatNSD is highly robust: while not always the top performer on individual datasets, it presents a substantially higher relative average improvement. Crucially, FlatNSD robustness may be explained by its general efficacy outside of purely over-squashing-dominated regimes. We highlight this perspective, recalling the discussion on Section B.2 about the existence of sheaves that mitigate over-smoothing and over-squashing simultaneously.

7 Related work

Sheaf Neural Networks. Building on the contributions of Bodnar et al. (2022), who demonstrated the advantages of the NSD model in handling heterophilic graphs and mitigating over-smoothing, we investigated the over-squashing phenomenon within SNNs. Bamberger et al. (2025) introduced flat vector bundles together with BuNN, an architecture that departs from the message-passing paradigm to address over-squashing. Our results suggest that the message-passing paradigm itself, when equipped with flat bundles, is already a strong contender: FlatNSD performs competitively with BuNN on the TreeNeighborsMatch task (Figure 1) and on node classification with larger graphs (Table 2). Notably, much of the variation across sheaf-based models seems to be explained by the choice of restriction-map parameterization rather than by the underlying architecture (Figure 1). Direct head-to-head comparisons remain limited as the BuNN code was not publicly available at the time of submission. Crucially, Ribeiro et al. (2026) introduced sheaves on directed graphs to allow a selective behavior of each node, creating the CSNN model, which also handles over-squashing. Other recently proposed sheaf-based models (Fiorini et al., 2026; Mule et al., 2026) also formulate directed sheaves but do not discuss data compression.

Graph Rewiring. Graph rewiring is a popular strategy to address over-squashing. Part of its success is theoretically explained by Di Giovanni et al. (2023) and empirically validated by different authors, using different heuristics Black et al. (2023); Topping et al. (2022); Karhadkar et al. (2023); Barbero et al. (2024); Liang et al. (2025). Moreover, relational GNNs are tools to improve rewiring methods that we exclude from our experiments, similarly to Nguyen et al. (2023); Liang et al. (2025). This choice intends to isolate the contribution of FlatNSD and to consider graph rewiring methods and SNNs without further performance-oriented modifications.

Over-squashing. There is a variety of strategies to overcome over-squashing and the related problem of long-range propagation. They include but do not restrict to: DE-GNN approaches (Gravina et al., 2025; Gravina et al., 2023), exploiting port-Hamiltonian dynamics (Heilig et al., 2025), adapting messages in the information flow (Errica et al., 2025; Finkelshtein et al., 2024), and Graph Transformers (Shirzad et al., 2023; Rampášek et al., 2022; Kreuzer et al., 2021). Our experiments establish SNNs as a principled member of this toolkit for mitigating over-squashing.

8 Conclusions

In this work, we established a theoretical link between Sheaf Neural Networks and over-squashing mitigation through the novel concept of Sheaf Effective Resistance. We demonstrated that FlatNSD can implicitly optimize restriction maps to facilitate information flow, all without altering the underlying graph topology. Our empirical analysis reveals that FlatNSD is a robust model, validating the efficacy of SNNs across diverse structural regimes.

Future works. Over-squashing is a well-known issue in GNNs, explored theoretically and empirically through various lenses. Many approaches rely on concepts deeply tied to effective resistance, such as the spectral gap, the Cheeger constant, and commute time. Notably, Topping et al. (2022) introduce an edge-based metric called Balanced Forman curvature, linking negatively curved edges to over-squashing and proving that a positive lower bound on curvature controls the spectral gap. We envision that defining a notion of curvature for graph sheaves could be intrinsically related to the sheaf spectral gap. This perspective further positions sheaves as a powerful tool to alleviate over-squashing: bottlenecks traditionally viewed as intrinsic to the graph structure might be better understood—and resolved—as properties of the associated sheaf.

Limitations. We recall that our goal with this work was to analyze how FlatNSD can deal with over-squashing. To this end, we keep the model as simple as possible. Our experiments and theoretical results contribute to support that sheaves, through the lens of sheaf effective resistance, provide a framework genuinely capable of mitigating over-squashing. Nevertheless, the FlatNSD model can be strengthened. For instance, Bamberger et al. (2025) considered a parallel dimension for multiple sheaves instead of a single sheaf per layer, which led to improved long-range interactions; Fiorini et al. (2026) generalizes the sheaf Laplacian even further with sheaves designed to explicitly account for directed graphs; Ribeiro et al. (2026) introduces a sheaf based model where each node can learn whether it propagates or receives messages from/to its neighbors in each layer.

Computational Complexity. Sheaf Neural Networks main drawback is its computational cost, but we address that the FlatNSD model we used in this work presents significant improvements in comparison to the original NSD model (Appendix G), showing positive perspectives in this realm. Nevertheless, in Appendix H we provide the runtime of FlatNSD and GCN with different rewiring methods, where we concluded that FlatNSD is considerable faster than graph rewiring methods for the tested node classification tasks while keeps the same order of magnitude for the tested graph classification tasks. This shows that FlatNSD is a versatile and balanced model.

Societal Impact. We foresee no immediate societal or ethical concerns arising from this work.

Appendix A Additional Examples

To give a better intuition of how the choice of sheaves affects effective resistance, we provide two larger examples, building on the graph effective resistance examples from Black et al. [2023].

Consider first the two graphs above: nodes a,ba,b connected by a path of length 66, and nodes a,ba,b connected by four disjoint paths of lengths 5,4,4,55,4,4,5. Their graph effective resistances are R⁡(a,b)=6R(a,b)=6 and R⁡(a,b)=109R(a,b)=\frac{10}{9}, respectively. From their Laplacian pseudo-inverses, we obtain (LG+)a​b=−87(L_{G}^{+})_{ab}=-\frac{8}{7} and (LG+)a​b=−1851152(L_{G}^{+})_{ab}=-\frac{185}{1152}.

Let Q⁡(k)=(cos⁡k−sin⁡ksin⁡kcos⁡k)Q(k)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos k&-\sin k\\ \sin k&\cos k\end{pmatrix}, and define ℱa=Q⁡(x){\mathcal{F}}_{a}=Q(x), ℱb=Q⁡(y){\mathcal{F}}_{b}=Q(y), with identity maps on all remaining nodes. Using Proposition 4.2, we obtain

Rℱ​(a,b)=52+32​cos⁡(y−x)7andRℱ​(a,b)=455+185​cos⁡(y−x)288,R_{{\mathcal{F}}}(a,b)=\frac{52+32\cos(y-x)}{7}\quad\text{and}\quad R_{{\mathcal{F}}}(a,b)=\frac{455+185\cos(y-x)}{288},

for the first and second graphs, respectively. Hence, for y−x∈{0,π2,π}y-x\in\{0,\frac{\pi}{2},\pi\}, we have

Rℱ​(a,b)∈{12,527,207}andRℱ​(a,b)∈{209,455288,1516},R_{{\mathcal{F}}}(a,b)\in\left\{12,\frac{52}{7},\frac{20}{7}\right\}\quad\text{and}\quad R_{{\mathcal{F}}}(a,b)\in\left\{\frac{20}{9},\frac{455}{288},\frac{15}{16}\right\},

for first and second graphs, respectively. Since (LG+)a​b<0(L_{G}^{+})_{ab}<0 in both cases, rotations can only lower the endpoint resistance relative to the aligned configuration.

Importantly, however, the effect of the sheaf need not be uniform throughout the graph. Let ww be the first internal node adjacent to aa in the path graph. In this case, (LG+)a​w=1(L_{G}^{+})_{aw}=1 and R⁡(a,w)=1R(a,w)=1, yielding Rℱ​(a,w)=6−4​cos⁡xR_{{\mathcal{F}}}(a,w)=6-4\cos x. Thus, every non-zero rotation at aa increases the resistance between aa and its neighbor. For example, taking ℱa=−I{\mathcal{F}}_{a}=-I and all other maps equal to the identity gives Rℱ​(a,b)=207R_{{\mathcal{F}}}(a,b)=\frac{20}{7} and Rℱ​(a,w)=10R_{{\mathcal{F}}}(a,w)=10, in contrast to Rℱ​(a,b)=12R_{{\mathcal{F}}}(a,b)=12 and Rℱ​(a,w)=2R_{{\mathcal{F}}}(a,w)=2 for the trivial sheaf. Therefore, a nontrivial sheaf can simultaneously lower the resistance between a distant pair while increasing it between nearby nodes. This is consistent with the role of the restriction maps: information can be transmitted efficiently from aa to bb even when it cannot be directly decoded by intermediate nodes along the communication path.

Appendix B Additional Experiments

B.1 Rewiring against FlatNSD on node classification

We additionally test the performance of FlatNSD against rewiring methods on the node classification benchmarks used in Nguyen et al. [2023], Liang et al. [2025]. It achieves the best performance in 4 out of 6 datasets, and a generally higher overall improvement of the backbone GNN compared to baselines. We notice that Cora and Citeseer are homophilic graphs, an environment where it is already known that sheaf-based models do not flourish Bodnar et al. [2022]. In contrast, graph rewiring techniques often struggle to improve their backbone GNNs on node classification tasks. This relates to the fact that graph rewiring methods primarily target over-squashing, whereas FlatNSD is more versatile.

Results. Table 3 shows that FlatNSD is a robust model across both node and graph classification tasks (Figure 5). The exceptions are Cora, Citeseer, and Chameleon. Cora and Citeseer are homophilic graphs, a regime where sheaf-based models are known to underperform their classical counterparts [Bodnar et al., 2022]; the drop relative to vanilla GCN on these datasets is therefore expected rather than surprising. Chameleon is known to contain duplicate nodes Platonov et al. [2023], which interfere with model performance. Overall, on the considered heterophilic datasets, FlatNSD is competitive with or superior to graph rewiring.

Effective Resistance. The Spearman correlation shows a weak correlation for these node classification. This aligns with the view that the graph classification tasks performed in Figure 5 is more suitable for studying over-squashing: it requires aggregating node information into a graph-level embedding, thereby amplifying information compression.

Accordingly, Saber and Salehi-Abari [2025] suggest that rewiring strategies primarily pay off when over-squashing is severe and global, but the standard node classification benchmarks used here likely suffer only from mild compression.Therefore, although this might attenuate the effectiveness of FlatNSD-SAGE regarding over-squashing mitigation on this set of problems, the model still achieves good performance in terms of raw accuracy, demonstrating its general efficacy outside of purely over-squashing-dominated regimes. We highlight this perspective, recalling the discussion on Section B.2 about the existence of sheaves that mitigate over-smoothing and over-squashing simultaneously.

B.2 Over-squashing and Over-smoothing

Most graph rewiring techniques address over-squashing by reducing effective resistance or, equivalently, enlarging the spectral gap and the Cheeger constant Black et al. [2023]. However, modifying the edge set of a graph also typically causes standard GNNs to yield increasingly similar node representations as the number of layers grows. In other words, mitigating over-squashing is often accompanied by a worsening of the over-smoothing effect.

To overcome this, R-GNNs are used instead of vanilla GNNs Karhadkar et al. [2023], Jamadandi et al. [2024]. Rougly speaking, R-GNNs models can keep information from the original graph and use it through learned weights to keep balance between over-squashing and over-smoothing.

On the other hand, it is well known that NSD can circumvent over-smoothing. The question is: are sheaves able to simultaneously mitigate over-squashing and over-smoothing?

For simplicity, we consider a connected graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) with nn vertices and two classes A,B⊆VA,B\subseteq V. Let αe\alpha_{e} for all e∈Ee\in E be arbitrary non-negative scalars. According to Bodnar et al. [2022, Proposition 10], a sheaf whose stalks have dimension one equipped with invertible restriction defined by

ℱv⊴e=−αe​ if ​v∈A​ and ​ℱu⊴e=αe​ if ​u∈B\mathcal{F}_{v\unlhd e}=-\alpha_{e}\mbox{ if }v\in A\mbox{ and }\mathcal{F}_{u\unlhd e}=\alpha_{e}\mbox{ if }u\in B (4)

induces a diffusion that can linearly separate the classes of GG for almost all initial conditions. Therefore, even if we increase the number of layers, in such circumstances, the feature nodes will not converge to the same value.

We show that equipping a graph with the sheaves above can also reduce the total effective resistance, consequently reducing network sensitivity to over-squashing by Theorem 4.1.

Theorem B.1.

Let GG be a connected graph with nn vertices and two classes A,B⊆VA,B\subseteq V. If ℱ{\mathcal{F}} is a flat vector bundle as in Equation 4, then Rℱ≤R\operatorname{R}_{{\mathcal{F}}}\leq\operatorname{R}.

Therefore, if the number of classes of GG is C=2C=2, there is a sheaf that handles both over-smoothing and over-squashing. For graphs with C>2C>2 classes, Bodnar et al. [2022] argued that sheaves whose stalks have dimension d≥Cd\geq C can mitigate over-smoothing. Our experiments in Figure 5 suggest that a higher dimensional version of the above theorem holds, since FlatNSD presents good performance on real-world datasets for node and graph classification tasks, where both over-smoothing and over-squashing may co-exist.

To substantiate the theoretical insight, we include experiments demonstrating that FlatNSD can handle over-smoothing and over-squashing simultaneously.

As explained by Alon and Yahav [2021], there is no reason to expect over-smoothing to occur in the TreeNeighborsMatch problem. To the best of our knowledge, there is no synthetic benchmark specifically designed to evaluate the ability of GNNs to cope with both over-squashing and over-smoothing. We therefore propose GridTransfer as a task to study this setting.

GridTransfer. We construct a graph by taking two n×nn\times n grids and adding a single edge that connects one node on the outermost diagonal of the first grid to one node on the outermost diagonal of the second grid. The task is to transfer information from a target node in the first grid to a node in the second grid located at the opposite corner relative to the endpoint of the inter-grid connection.

The nodes along the main diagonal of each grid act as green nodes, as in the NeighborsMatch task, and each green node is connected to a number of blue neighbors. The label is determined by matching the number of blue neighbors: the green node whose number of blue neighbors equals that of the target node contains its true label.

We adopt the same model configurations as in TreeNeighborsMatch and choose the network depth as 4​(n−1)+14(n-1)+1, which corresponds to the worst-case receptive-field requirement for transferring information across the two-grid construction. Since this depth increases linearly with nn, larger grids induce much deeper networks, where over-smoothing is expected to be more pronounced. Results are shown in Figure 9. In comparison with TreeNeighborsMatch, we observe that FlatNSD-SAGE remains robust, indicating that over-smoothing has limited impact on its performance in this setting.

Dirichlet Energy. Cai and Wang [2020] used Dirichlet energy, given by the quadratic form EG​(𝐗)≔tr⁡(𝐗⊤​ΔG​𝐗)E_{G}(\mathbf{X})\coloneqq\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\Delta_{G}\mathbf{X}), where ΔG\Delta_{G} is the normalized Laplacian of the graph GG, as a measure of “smoothness” of node embeddings.

From the perspective of Laplacian smoothing, deeper GCN propagation increasingly favors low-frequency signals, which generally lowers the Dirichlet energy and may cause node embeddings to become nearly constant on each connected component. Hence, mitigating over-smoothing should manifest as maintaining higher Dirichlet energy across layers, or equivalently, a less pronounced decrease.

In Figure 10, we observe that FlatNSD with restriction maps learned with a GCN increases the energy for Enzymes, IMDB, MUTAG, and Proteins. We find consistent empirical evidence that the learned restriction maps are associated with decreasing sheaf effective resistance during training in regimes sensitive to over-squashing. While this does not establish causality, it supports the theoretical link between resistance and information propagation and provides a diagnostic for when FlatNSD alleviates over-squashing – whilst still alleviating over-smoothing through the increase of the Dirichlet energy.

B.3 Evaluating FlatNSD on Graph Transfer

The Graph Transfer task proposed by Di Giovanni et al. [2023] as a benchmark for over-squashing, evaluates a model’s ability to propagate information from a target node to a source node. The task is defined on three graph topologies: Ring, CrossedRing, and CliquePath, where rr denotes the distance between the source and the target node.

Ring graphs are simple cycles of size nn in which the source and target nodes lie at distance ⌊n/2⌋\lfloor n/2\rfloor. CrossedRing graphs are cycles of the same size augmented with chords/crosses between auxiliary nodes; the added edges do not shorten the source–target distance, which remains ⌊n/2⌋\lfloor n/2\rfloor. CliquePath graphs consist of a ⌊n/2⌋\lfloor n/2\rfloor-clique connected to a path of length ⌊n/2⌋\lfloor n/2\rfloor, with the source placed inside the clique and the target at the far end of the path; the source–target distance is ⌊n/2⌋+1\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1. The three topologies are designed to isolate the effect of structural connectivity at a fixed distance: although rr is matched across topologies, over-squashing is most severe for CliquePath and least severe for CrossedRing.

Results. For all three topologies, FlatNSD can postpone the accuracy drop, i.e., in FlatNSD accuracy decreases only after bigger distances from source to target, in comparison with all non-sheaf based models (GAT, GCN, GIN, SAGE), providing further evidence that FlatNSD mitigates over-squashing. Moreover, d=4d=4 presents better performance than d=2d=2, suggesting the importance of stalk dimension dd for tasks sensitive to over-squashing, in alignment with our results for the TreeNeighborsMatch task.

B.4 Spearman Correlation on the TreeNeighborsMatch task

Recall that Spearman correlation assesses the monotonic relationship between two variables and yields a value in [−1,1][-1,1].

Accuracy. We compute Spearman rank correlation per layer between training accuracy in the TreeNeighborsMatch and the sheaf effective resistance across all radii rr with d=4d=4. While the model does not consistently recover the resistance-minimizing sheaf at each layer, it reliably does so in the initial layers.

The effective resistance reported in Figure 2 and Figure 12 is the mean of total sheaf effective resistance throughout the batches in each epoch, for each layer. The correlation is then calculated over the pairs (m​e​a​n​(Rℱb​a​t​c​h​e​s),t​r​a​i​n​a​c​c)(mean(R_{{\mathcal{F}}}^{batches}),train~acc).

Jacobian norm. Still in the TreeNeighborsMatch, we compute Spearman rank correlation between the Jacobian norm and the sheaf effective resistance. As predicted by the theory, we obtained a strong negative correlation between them. Moreover, the plots showing correlation with the Jacobian (Figure 13) and the plots showing correlation with accuracy (Figure 12) exhibit the same behavior. This result further supports the hypothesis that a reduction in sheaf effective resistance enhances the Jacobian sensitivity, thereby assisting in the mitigation of over-squashing.

B.5 Short-range Over-squashing

Mishayev et al. [2025] proposes a short-range over-squashing scenario, instantiated through the two-radius problem. In their experiments, SetTransformer achieves 100% accuracy across all tested graph sizes, while message-passing GNNs struggle to fit the data, with GAT being the best-performing architecture among GCN, GIN, and SAGE. We evaluate FlatNSD on the same task, fixing d=2d=2 and the remaining parameters as in Mishayev et al. [2025]. Notably, FlatNSD with a SetTransformer backbone and hidden dimension 32 achieves 100% accuracy across all graph sizes, with fast convergence (under 35 epochs).

To better isolate the contribution of the sheaf, we also evaluate FlatNSD with a SAGE backbone. Its performance starts to decay on the two-radius problem with 50 nodes, but remains above that of SAGE alone. This highlights the importance of choosing an appropriate parametrization for the backbone GNN, revealing a similar dichotomy to that observed between the parametrizations used in the TreeNeighborsMatch experiment.

B.6 Intervention on the TreeNeighborsMatch problem

To examine the distinction between correlation and mechanism more directly, we perform a controlled intervention on TreeNeighborsMatch with fixed stalk dimension. We compare a trivial flat bundle, with ℱv=Id{\mathcal{F}}_{v}=I_{d} at every node, against an oracle endpoint intervention in which all maps remain fixed to the identity except those at the root and the task-relevant leaf.

The trivial bundle attains the maximum possible total resistance. Under this configuration, the model fails to fit the training set, remaining near 0.0450.045 training accuracy. By contrast, allowing nontrivial maps only at the two task-relevant endpoints substantially lowers their pairwise sheaf effective resistance, and the model converges almost immediately, after only two iterations. Since the graph topology and all remaining restriction maps are unchanged, this controlled intervention shows that modifying the flat bundle can remove a communication obstruction that persists under the maximum-resistance trivial bundle. This provides more direct evidence for the role of sheaf effective resistance in the mechanism underlying information propagation, beyond the correlation observed during learning.

Appendix C Contributions and the role of FlatNSD

The main contributions of this work are theoretical rather than architectural. In particular, we derive a closed-form expression for pairwise sheaf effective resistance for flat bundles (Proposition 4.2), a closed-form expression for total sheaf effective resistance, together with an efficient way of computing it (Theorem 4.2), and establish a connection between sheaf effective resistance and bounds on the message-passing Jacobian (Theorems 4.1 and 4.1). We further extend Theorem 2.1, Theorem 4.1, and Corollary 4.1 to bipartite graphs by extending the corresponding results for graph effective resistance (Lemma 4.1, Proposition 4.4, and Theorem 4.3). We also provide a result characterizing the existence of flat bundles that strictly decrease effective resistance (Proposition 4.3) and empirically study how sheaf effective resistance evolves during learning. FlatNSD is introduced as a simplified model used to isolate and verify these mechanisms empirically, rather than as the main contribution of the paper.

Our analysis builds upon several existing results. Sheaf effective resistance was introduced by Hansen and Ghrist [2019]; our contribution is to recognize and develop its use as a tool for understanding information propagation in sheaf-based GNNs. We further build upon the flat sheaf Laplacian decomposition of Bamberger et al. [2025], the connection between graph effective resistance and message-passing Jacobian bounds developed by Black et al. [2023], and the Neural Sheaf Diffusion (NSD) architecture of Bodnar et al. [2022]. The results developed here combine these ingredients to connect the geometry of learned sheaves, effective resistance, and over-squashing.

To further clarify the role of FlatNSD, we briefly compare it with the sheaf-based architectures considered throughout this work. FlatNSD intentionally removes architectural components that are not necessary for studying the resistance mechanism, while retaining the basic sheaf diffusion structure:

  • •

    FlatNSD: learns one orthogonal map ℱv{\mathcal{F}}_{v} per vertex vv and uses the same diffusion process as NSD. The resulting sheaf is a flat O⁡(d)O(d)-bundle, which allows the decomposition Lℱ=𝐎⊤​(LG⊗Id)​𝐎L_{{\mathcal{F}}}={\mathbf{O}}^{\top}(L_{G}\otimes I_{d}){\mathbf{O}} and makes the theoretical analysis particularly transparent.

  • •

    Orthogonal NSD: learns one orthogonal restriction map ℱv⊴e{\mathcal{F}}_{v\unlhd e} for each vertex-edge incidence pair v⊴ev\unlhd e. Its diffusion operator is the sheaf Laplacian obtained from the discretized heat equation on the sheaf. FlatNSD can be viewed as a constrained version of this construction in which the incidence maps are induced by a single map per node.

  • •

    BuNN: also learns one orthogonal map ℱv{\mathcal{F}}_{v} per vertex, but uses the corresponding heat kernel as its diffusion operator. It therefore shares the same flat-bundle parameterization while differing in how diffusion is performed.

  • •

    CSNN: learns two conformal maps 𝐒v{\mathbf{S}}_{v} and 𝐓v{\mathbf{T}}_{v} for each node and constructs the sheaf on a directed graph. Its diffusion operator is formed from a product of in- and out-Laplacians, making it more expressive and structurally different from the flat orthogonal setting considered in our analysis.

These distinctions are important for interpreting the experimental results. FlatNSD is not proposed as a replacement for more expressive sheaf-based architectures. Instead, its restricted parameterization provides a controlled setting in which the theoretical predictions can be tested with as few additional mechanisms as possible. In this sense, FlatNSD serves as a basic sheaf model for validating the relationship between learned sheaf geometry, effective resistance, and over-squashing, while architectures such as NSD, BuNN, and CSNN incorporate additional modeling choices that may affect performance beyond this mechanism.

Appendix D More about sheaf effective resistance

Hansen and Ghrist [2019] introduced cosheaf effective resistance on a cell complex11 1 A graph is a 11-dimensional cell complex. Cellular sheaves can be defined in this more general context, but considering them into GNNs realm brings complications we do not discuss in this work.. Here, we adapt their definition to a graph GG with nn vertices and ℱ{\mathcal{F}} a sheaf over GG whose stalks have dimension d.d.

Definition D.1.

The sheaf effective resistance between nodes uu and vv is given by the solution to the optimization problem

minc∈C1​(G,ℱ)⁡‖c‖2​s.t​δ⊤​c=𝟙u−𝟙v,\min\limits_{c\in C^{1}(G,{\mathcal{F}})}\|c\|^{2}\,\,\,\,\mbox{s.t}\,\,\,\,\delta^{\top}c=\mathbbm{1}_{u}-\mathbbm{1}_{v}, (5)

where 𝟙v\mathbbm{1}_{v} is a binary vector of length n​dnd where only the dd entries corresponding to node vv is 11.

If the sheaf is trivial, then the effective resistance is the solution to min⁡{‖c‖2∣B​c=1u−1v}\min\{\|c\|^{2}\mid Bc=1_{u}-1_{v}\}, where BB is the incidence matrix of GG. This is equivalent to R⁡(u,v)=(1u−1v)⊤​LG+​(1u−1v).\operatorname{R}(u,v)=(1_{u}-1_{v})^{\top}L^{+}_{G}(1_{u}-1_{v}).

We check the equivalence between Definition D.1 and Definition 4.1 in the following proposition:

Proposition D.1.

Definition D.1 and Definition 4.1 are equivalent.

Proof.

Recall that for any matrix A⊤​AA^{\top}A, it holds that x⊤​(A⊤​A)+​x=min⁡{‖y‖2∣A⊤​y=x}x^{\top}(A^{\top}A)^{+}x=\operatorname{min}\{\|y\|^{2}\mid A^{\top}y=x\}. Moreover, Lℱ=δ⊤​δL_{{\mathcal{F}}}=\delta^{\top}\delta. Consequently:

Rℱ⁡(u,v)\displaystyle\operatorname{R}_{{\mathcal{F}}}(u,v) =(𝟙u−𝟙v)⊤​Lℱ+​(𝟙u−𝟙v)\displaystyle=(\mathbbm{1}_{u}-\mathbbm{1}_{v})^{\top}L_{{\mathcal{F}}}^{+}(\mathbbm{1}_{u}-\mathbbm{1}_{v})
=min⁡{‖c‖2∣δ⊤​c=(𝟙u−𝟙v)}.\displaystyle=\operatorname{min}\{\|c\|^{2}\mid\delta^{\top}c=(\mathbbm{1}_{u}-\mathbbm{1}_{v})\}.

∎

In this work we also consider the total sheaf effective resistance, which Rℱ\operatorname{R}_{{\mathcal{F}}} is the sum of the sheaf effective resistance Rℱ⁡(u,v)\operatorname{R}_{{\mathcal{F}}}(u,v) for all pairs of nodes. With vertex-major indexing, write Lℱ+L_{\mathcal{F}}^{+} as n2n^{2} blocks (Lℱ+)i​j(L_{\mathcal{F}}^{+})^{ij}, each of dimension d×dd\times d in the following way:

Lℱ+=((Lℱ+)11…(Lℱ+)1​n⋱(Lℱ+)n​1…(Lℱ+)n​n),L_{{\mathcal{F}}}^{+}=\begin{pmatrix}(L_{{\mathcal{F}}}^{+})^{11}&\dots&(L_{{\mathcal{F}}}^{+})^{1n}\\ \vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ (L_{{\mathcal{F}}}^{+})^{n1}&\dots&(L_{{\mathcal{F}}}^{+})^{nn}\end{pmatrix},

then a straightforward calculation leads to:

Proposition D.2.

Let ⟨⋅,⋅⟩F\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{F} denote the Frobenius inner product, and 1 denote a matrix whose entries are all equal to one. Let ℱ{\mathcal{F}} be a sheaf over a connected graph GG. Then

Rℱ=(n−1)​∑i∈V⟨(Lℱ+)i​i,1⟩F−2​∑i<j⟨(Lℱ+)i​j,1⟩F,\operatorname{R}_{{\mathcal{F}}}=(n-1)\sum\limits_{i\in V}\langle(L^{+}_{{\mathcal{F}}})^{ii},\textbf{1}\rangle_{F}-2\sum\limits_{i<j}\langle(L^{+}_{{\mathcal{F}}})^{ij},\textbf{1}\rangle_{F},

where 1∈ℝn×n\textbf{1}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n\times n} is a matrix of ones.

Proof.

Here we use a numerical index notation i,ji,j, which we believe will help to follow the argument.

Observe that Rℱ​(i,j)=∑k,l=1d((Lℱ+)k​li​i+(Lℱ+)k​lj​j)−2​∑k,l=1d(Lℱ+)k​li​jR_{{\mathcal{F}}}(i,j)=\sum\limits_{k,l=1}^{d}\left((L_{{\mathcal{F}}}^{+})^{ii}_{kl}+(L_{{\mathcal{F}}}^{+})^{jj}_{kl}\right)-2\sum\limits_{k,l=1}^{d}(L_{{\mathcal{F}}}^{+})^{ij}_{kl}, for each pair of nodes i,j∈Vi,j\in V.

To calculate the sheaf effective resistance we need sum all Rℱ​(i,j)R_{{\mathcal{F}}}(i,j). So

Rℱ\displaystyle R_{{\mathcal{F}}} =(n−1)​(∑i​j=1d(Lℱ+)i​j11+⋯+∑i​j=1d(Lℱ+)i​jn​n)−2​(∑i​j=1d(Lℱ+)i​j12+⋯+(Lℱ+)i​j1​n)\displaystyle=(n-1)\left(\sum\limits_{ij=1}^{d}(L_{{\mathcal{F}}}^{+})^{11}_{ij}+\dots+\sum\limits_{ij=1}^{d}(L_{{\mathcal{F}}}^{+})^{nn}_{ij}\right)-2\left(\sum\limits_{ij=1}^{d}(L_{{\mathcal{F}}}^{+})^{12}_{ij}+\dots+(L_{{\mathcal{F}}}^{+})^{1n}_{ij}\right)
−2​((Lℱ+)i​j23+(Lℱ+)i​j2​n)−⋯−2​∑i​j=1d(Lℱ+)i​jn−1​n\displaystyle-2\left((L_{{\mathcal{F}}}^{+})^{23}_{ij}+(L_{{\mathcal{F}}}^{+})^{2n}_{ij}\right)-\dots-2\sum\limits_{ij=1}^{d}(L_{{\mathcal{F}}}^{+})^{n-1n}_{ij}
=(n−1)​∑i∈V⟨(Lℱ+)i​i,1⟩F−2​∑i<j⟨(Lℱ+)i​j,1⟩F.\displaystyle=(n-1)\sum\limits_{i\in V}\langle(L^{+}_{{\mathcal{F}}})^{ii},\textbf{1}\rangle_{F}-2\sum\limits_{i<j}\langle(L^{+}_{{\mathcal{F}}})^{ij},\textbf{1}\rangle_{F}.

∎

Theorem 4.2. Let ⟨⋅,⋅⟩F\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{F} denote the Frobenius inner product and define MM as in Proposition 4.2. Then

Rℱ=d​n​Tr⁡(LG+)−⟨M,LG+⟩F=d​R−⟨M,LG+⟩F\operatorname{R}_{\mathcal{F}}=dn\operatorname{Tr}(L_{G}^{+})-\langle M,L_{G}^{+}\rangle_{F}=d\operatorname{R}-\langle M,L_{G}^{+}\rangle_{F}
Proof.

On one hand, by Proposition 4.2, we have

Rℱ\displaystyle\operatorname{R}_{\mathcal{F}} =d​∑u<v((LG+)u​u+(LG+)v​v)−2​∑u<vMu​v​(LG+)u​v\displaystyle=d\sum_{u<v}\left((L_{G}^{+})_{uu}+(L_{G}^{+})_{vv}\right)-2\sum_{u<v}M_{uv}(L_{G}^{+})_{uv}
=d⁡(n−1)​∑u∈V(LG+)u​u−2​∑u<vMu​v​(LG+)u​v\displaystyle=d(n-1)\sum_{u\in V}(L_{G}^{+})_{uu}-2\sum_{u<v}M_{uv}(L_{G}^{+})_{uv}
=d⁡(n−1)​Tr⁡(LG+)−2​∑u<vMu​v​(LG+)u​v\displaystyle=d(n-1)\operatorname{Tr}(L_{G}^{+})-2\sum_{u<v}M_{uv}(L_{G}^{+})_{uv}

On the other hand, observe that

⟨M,LG+⟩F=∑u,v∈VMu​v​(LG+)u​v\displaystyle\langle M,L_{G}^{+}\rangle_{F}=\sum\limits_{u,v\in V}M_{uv}(L^{+}_{G})_{uv} =∑u∈VMu​u​(LG+)u​u+∑u≠vMu​v​(LG+)u​v\displaystyle=\sum\limits_{u\in V}M_{uu}(L^{+}_{G})_{uu}+\sum\limits_{u\neq v}M_{uv}(L^{+}_{G})_{uv}

where u<vu<v means we are considering only the upper triangular part of the matrix, and the equality holds because both LG+L^{+}_{G} and MM are symmetric. Thus

Proposition 4.3. Let GG be a connected graph with at least two nodes and ℱ{\mathcal{F}} a flat O⁡(d)O(d)-bundle over GG. Then Rℱd≤R\frac{R_{{\mathcal{F}}}}{d}\leq R, with equality holding if and only if ℱv​𝟏d=c{\mathcal{F}}_{v}\mathbf{1}_{d}=c for some c∈ℝdc\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} and all v∈Vv\in V. In particular, for every d≥1d\geq 1, there exists a flat O⁡(d)O(d)-bundle ℱ{\mathcal{F}} such that Rℱd<R\frac{R_{{\mathcal{F}}}}{d}<R.

Proof.

Recall that SS is a matrix with Su=𝟏d⊤​ℱu⊤S_{u}=\mathbf{1}_{d}^{\top}{\mathcal{F}}_{u}^{\top} and M=S​S⊤M=SS^{\top}, therefore

⟨M,LG+⟩=Tr⁡(S⊤​LG+​S)≥0,\langle M,L_{G}^{+}\rangle=\Tr(S^{\top}L_{G}^{+}S)\geq 0,

since LG+⪰0L_{G}^{+}\succeq 0, and then Rℱd≤R\frac{R_{{\mathcal{F}}}}{d}\leq R by Theorem 4.2. If the underlying graph GG is connected, ker⁡LG=(𝟏n)\ker L_{G}=(\mathbf{1}_{n}), thus Rℱd=R\frac{R_{{\mathcal{F}}}}{d}=R precisely when ℱv​𝟏d=c{\mathcal{F}}_{v}\mathbf{1}_{d}=c, for some c∈ℝdc\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} and all v∈Vv\in V. Therefore the inequality is strict whenever ℱv​𝟏d{\mathcal{F}}_{v}\mathbf{1}_{d} is non-constant. We proceed to show a family of sheaves for which effective resistance is decreased.

Consider any non-trivial vertex partition V=A⊔BV=A\sqcup B and define εv={+1,v∈A,−1,v∈B\varepsilon_{v}=\begin{cases}+1,&v\in A,\\ -1,&v\in B\end{cases}. Lemma 4.1. Let GG be a connected bipartite graph. Then ΔG+=12​P−+∑k=0∞(A^k−P+−(−1)k​P−)\Delta_{G}^{+}=\frac{1}{2}P_{-}+\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(\hat{A}^{k}-P_{+}-(-1)^{k}P_{-}), where P+P_{+} and P−P_{-} are the outer product of the eigenvectors with eigenvalues 11 and −1-1, respectively.

The kernel of the Laplacian is ker⁡LG=(𝟏n)\ker L_{G}=(\mathbf{1}_{n}), and the symmetrically normalized Laplacian is ΔG=I−D−1/2AD−1/2=I−A^\Delta_{G}=I-D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}=I-\hat{A}. Thus

x∈ker⁡ΔG⇔(I−A^)​x=0⇔A^​x=x.x\in\ker\Delta_{G}\iff(I-\hat{A})x=0\iff\hat{A}x=x.

We also have

x∈kerΔG⇔D−1/2LGD−1/2x=0⇔LG(D−1/2x)=0⇔D−1/2x∈kerLG.x\in\ker\Delta_{G}\iff D^{-1/2}L_{G}D^{-1/2}x=0\iff L_{G}(D^{-1/2}x)=0\iff D^{-1/2}x\in\ker L_{G}.

We conclude that if x∈ker⁡ΔGx\in\ker\Delta_{G}, then x=c​D1/2​𝟏nx=cD^{1/2}\mathbf{1}_{n}, and therefore the normalized eigenvector of A^\hat{A} corresponding to the eigenvalue 1 is q+=D1/2​𝟏nvol⁡(G)q_{+}=\frac{D^{1/2}\mathbf{1}_{n}}{\sqrt{\operatorname{vol}(G)}}. Now let (u,v)∈E(u,v)\in E, then εu=−εv\varepsilon_{u}=-\varepsilon_{v}, thus

(A​ε)v=∑u∈𝒩⁡(v)εu=−dv​εv,(A\varepsilon)_{v}=\sum_{u\in{\mathcal{N}}(v)}\varepsilon_{u}=-d_{v}\varepsilon_{v},

i.e. A​ε=−D​εA\varepsilon=-D\varepsilon. This yields

A^D1/2ε=D−1/2Aε=D−1/2(−Dε)=−D1/2ε,\hat{A}D^{1/2}\varepsilon=D^{-1/2}A\varepsilon=D^{-1/2}(-D\varepsilon)=-D^{1/2}\varepsilon,

and we conclude that the normalized eigenvector with eigenvalue −1-1 is q−=D1/2​εvol⁡(G)q_{-}=\frac{D^{1/2}\varepsilon}{\sqrt{\operatorname{vol}(G)}}. Defining P+=q+​q+⊤P_{+}=q_{+}q_{+}^{\top}, P−=q−​q−⊤P_{-}=q_{-}q_{-}^{\top} and Pi=qi​qi⊤P_{i}=q_{i}q_{i}^{\top}, where the qq’s are the eigenvectors of A^\hat{A}, we get

A^=Q​diag⁡(1,−1,μ2,…,μn−1)​Q⊤=P+−P−+∑i=2n−1μi​Pi.\hat{A}=Q\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,\mu_{2},\dots,\mu_{n-1})\>Q^{\top}=P_{+}-P_{-}+\sum_{i=2}^{n-1}\mu_{i}P_{i}.

Furthermore, since B={q+,q−,q2,…,qn−1}B=\{q_{+},q_{-},q_{2},\dots,q_{n-1}\} forms an orthonormal basis, we get I=P++P−+∑i=2n−1PiI=P_{+}+P_{-}+\sum_{i=2}^{n-1}P_{i}, therefore

ΔG=I−A^=2​P−+∑i=2n−1(1−μi)​Pi⟹ΔG+=12​P−+∑i=2n−111−μi​Pi.\Delta_{G}=I-\hat{A}=2P_{-}+\sum_{i=2}^{n-1}(1-\mu_{i})P_{i}\implies\Delta_{G}^{+}=\frac{1}{2}P_{-}+\sum_{i=2}^{n-1}\frac{1}{1-\mu_{i}}P_{i}.

Since |μi|<1|\mu_{i}|<1, we have 11−μi=∑k=0∞μik\frac{1}{1-\mu_{i}}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu_{i}^{k}, thus

ΔG+=12​P−+∑i=2n−1∑k=0∞μik​Pi=12​P−+∑k=0∞∑i=2n−1μik​Pi.\Delta_{G}^{+}=\frac{1}{2}P_{-}+\sum_{i=2}^{n-1}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu_{i}^{k}P_{i}=\frac{1}{2}P_{-}+\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\sum_{i=2}^{n-1}\mu_{i}^{k}P_{i}.

But A^k=P++(−1)k​P−+∑i=2n−1μik​Pi⟹∑i=2n−1μik​Pi=A^k−P+−(−1)k​P−\hat{A}^{k}=P_{+}+(-1)^{k}P_{-}+\sum_{i=2}^{n-1}\mu_{i}^{k}P_{i}\implies\sum_{i=2}^{n-1}\mu_{i}^{k}P_{i}=\hat{A}^{k}-P_{+}-(-1)^{k}P_{-}, which yields

≤dmax2​(∑k=0r((A^k)u​udu+(A^k)v​vdv)+12​γu​v−R⁡(u,v)+2dmin​μ¯r+11−μ¯)\displaystyle\leq\frac{d_{\max}}{2}\left(\sum_{k=0}^{r}\left(\frac{(\hat{A}^{k})_{uu}}{d_{u}}+\frac{(\hat{A}^{k})_{vv}}{d_{v}}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\gamma_{uv}-R(u,v)+\frac{2}{d_{\min}}\frac{\overline{\mu}^{r+1}}{1-\overline{\mu}}\right)

Notice that

|(A^k)u​u|=|𝟙u⊤​A^k​𝟙u|≤‖𝟙u⊤‖2​‖A^k‖2​‖𝟙u‖2≤‖A^k‖2,|(\hat{A}^{k})_{uu}|=|\mathbbm{1}_{u}^{\top}\hat{A}^{k}\mathbbm{1}_{u}|\leq\|\mathbbm{1}_{u}^{\top}\|_{2}\|\hat{A}^{k}\|_{2}\|\mathbbm{1}_{u}\|_{2}\leq\|\hat{A}^{k}\|_{2},

∑k=0r((A^k)u​udu+(A^k)v​vdv)≤∑k=0r(1du+1dv)≤∑k=0r2dmin=2dmin​(r+1).\sum_{k=0}^{r}\left(\frac{(\hat{A}^{k})_{uu}}{d_{u}}+\frac{(\hat{A}^{k})_{vv}}{d_{v}}\right)\leq\sum_{k=0}^{r}\left(\frac{1}{d_{u}}+\frac{1}{d_{v}}\right)\leq\sum_{k=0}^{r}\frac{2}{d_{\min}}=\frac{2}{d_{\min}}(r+1).

We conclude that

∑k=0r(A^k)u​v≤dmax2​(2dmin​(r+1+μ¯r+11−μ¯)+12​γu​v−R⁡(u,v)).\sum_{k=0}^{r}(\hat{A}^{k})_{uv}\leq\frac{d_{\max}}{2}\left(\frac{2}{d_{\min}}\left(r+1+\frac{\overline{\mu}^{r+1}}{1-\overline{\mu}}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\gamma_{uv}-R(u,v)\right).

Plugging this into Lemma 3.2 of Black et al. [2023] yields the desired inequality. ∎

Appendix F Experimental details

In this section, we provide additional details on the experimental setup, such as hyperparameter configurations and computational resources. For the real-world datasets related to over-squashing, we choose d∈{2,3,4,5}d\in\{2,3,4,5\}, three options of GNN architectures to learn restriction maps — GCN, GIN, and SAGE — with ℓGNN∈{1,2,3,4,5}\ell_{\operatorname{GNN}}\in\{1,2,3,4,5\}. We perform grid search for the hyperparameter configurations reported in Table 4.

For the ECHO-Synth benchmarks, we reproduce the experimental setup of Miglior et al. [2025], performing Bayesian Optimization based on a GP prior in the chosen hyperparameter space. We fix the same range for hidden dimension, learning rate and weight decay proposed by the authors, layers from 10 to 40, stalk dimension and number of layers for a fixed SAGE backbone from 2 to 6, and backbone hidden dimension from 4 to 64.

Compute resources. Hyperparameter search for Table 2 was performed on an internal cluster equipped with NVIDIA V100, A100, and H100 GPUs. Experiments for Table 3 and Figure 5 were run on a node with an Intel Xeon CPU (12 cores @ 2.20GHz) and a single NVIDIA A100-SXM4 (80GB) GPU. The remaining experiments were carried out on a workstation with two NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 (24GB).

Appendix G Computational Complexity

Here we compare the time complexity of FlatNSD against the time complexity of NSD with orthogonal maps. Let nn be the number of vertices, mm the number of edges, dd the dimension of the stalks, hh the number of channels, and c=d×hc=d\times h dimension.

NSD. Bodnar et al. [2022] shows that the time complexity of NSD with orthogonal restrictions maps is 𝐎⁡(𝐧⁡(𝐜𝟐+𝐝𝟑)+𝐦⁡(𝐜𝐝𝟐+𝐝𝟑))\mathbf{O(n(c^{2}+d^{3})+m(cd^{2}+d^{3}))}, where d∈{1,2,3,4,5}d\in\{1,2,3,4,5\}.

Importantly, Bodnar et al. [2022] learns orthogonal maps from a composition of Householder reflections Mhammedi et al. [2017]. We use the same strategy to build the orthogonal maps in FlatNSD.

FlatNSD. We derive the time complexity of FlatNSD as follows: we need O⁡(d2​n)O(d^{2}n) to embed graph features in the sheaf stalks, O⁡(m​c​d)O(mcd) for the message-passing, O⁡(n​c​d)O(ncd) whenever we apply W1W_{1}, and O⁡(n​c​h)O(nch) whenever we apply W2W_{2}.

Thus, the total time complexity is 𝐎⁡(𝐜𝐧⁡(𝐝+𝐡)+𝐦𝐜𝐝)\mathbf{O(cn(d+h)+mcd)}, where d∈{2,3,4,5}d\in\{2,3,4,5\}.

The computational gain of FlatNSD comes from learning a single restriction map to each node instead of two restriction maps to each edges (i.e., we have flat vector bundles instead of merely vector bundles), and from an optimized implementation based on message-passing.

Appendix H Runtime Comparison

We provide Table 5 to compare the total runtime of FlatNSD against GCN coupled with seven graph rewiring strategies. On node classification benchmarks, FlatNSD exhibits superior efficiency, reducing runtime by up to 5×5\times on dense datasets like Chameleon compared to SDRF. Regarding graph classification tasks (Enzymes, IMDB, Mutag, and Proteins), while FlatNSD incurs a higher computational cost due to per-graph processing overhead, its total runtime remains within the same order of magnitude as the baseline methods.
